\chapter{Sorry}
\label{ch:te-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can apologise in Telugu and ask someone to forgive me, using the same respectful ending.}

Say \te{క్షమించండి}, unpack it as kṣamin̄cu plus the respectful -aṇḍi already met in kūrcōṇḍi, and trace it to Sanskrit kṣamā.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\te{క్షమించండి}]{\te{క్షమించండి} — sorry}

\label{lesson:TE-C09-kshaminchandi}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} and its respectful \textbf{‑\te{ండి}} ending (\emph{kūrcōṇḍi}, \textquotedblleft{}please sit\textquotedblright{}). Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} hands you that very ending again, riding a brand-new verb.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{క్షమా}} (\emph{kṣamā}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{forgiveness, patience}\textquotedblright{} — the Sanskrit noun, borrowed whole.
  \item \textbf{‑\te{ఇంచు}} (\emph{‑in̄cu}) = a \textbf{verb-making suffix}: \emph{kṣamā} + \emph{‑in̄cu} $\to$ \textbf{\te{క్షమించు}} (\emph{kṣamin̄cu}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to forgive}.\textquotedblright{} (The same pattern gives \te{ప్రారంభించు} \emph{prārambhin̄cu}, \textquotedblleft{}to begin,\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \emph{prārambha}.)
  \item \textbf{‑\te{ండి}} (\emph{‑aṇḍi}) = the \textbf{respectful imperative} ending — exactly the one you already met on \emph{kūrcōṇḍi} \textquotedblleft{}please sit\textquotedblright{} and \emph{ceppaṇḍi} \textquotedblleft{}please tell me.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{please forgive}\textquotedblright{} — the same polite mold you already know, filled with a new verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Telugu \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} \emph{kṣamin̄\textbf{caṇḍi}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑in̄cu} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇḍi} (imperative)
  \item Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{si}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑isu} (verb) + \textbf{‑i} (imperative)
  \item Malayalam \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{kkaṇaṁ}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣama} + \textbf{‑ikkuka} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇaṁ} (necessitative)
  \item Tamil \textbf{\ta{மன்னிக்கவும்}} \emph{maṉṉi\textbf{kkavum}} — its \textbf{own} native root \emph{maṉṉi}, not Sanskrit at all
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} is a real, everyday \textquotedblleft{}sorry / please forgive me\textquotedblright{} — not stiffly formal — though in quick, casual exchanges Telugu speakers just as often reach for the borrowed English \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kṣamā\textquotedblright{} — the Sanskrit noun, forgiveness
  \item the verb — \textquotedblleft{}kṣamin̄cu,\textquotedblright{} to forgive — then \textquotedblleft{}kṣamin̄caṇḍi,\textquotedblright{} please forgive
  \item the ending you already know — \textquotedblleft{}‑aṇḍi,\textquotedblright{} same as kūrcōṇḍi
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} built from? (\textbf{Sanskrit kṣamā} + the verb-making suffix \textbf{‑in̄cu} + the respectful ending \textbf{‑aṇḍi}, which you already met on \emph{kūrcōṇḍi}.) Which cousins also verb-ify \emph{kṣamā}, and which doesn't? (\textbf{Kannada and Malayalam} do too; \textbf{Tamil} uses its own root \emph{maṉṉi}.) What's the casual alternative? (\textbf{Borrowed English \textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{}})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anusvara]{\te{◌ం} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S04-sign-anusvara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{క} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ం}}
\textbf{\te{◌ం}} — \emph{a nasal, ridden on the syllable before it}.

It is a \textbf{nasal}, written as a mark rather than as a letter. It rides on the syllable before it and turns the end of it nasal.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌ం} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{రేపు} \te{కలుద్దాం}} \emph{rēpu kaluddām} — see you tomorrow
  \item \textbf{\te{మళ్ళీ} \te{కలుద్దాం}} \emph{maḷḷī kaluddām} — we'll meet again
  \item \textbf{\te{ఉండు}} \emph{uṇḍu} — to be, to stay, to live
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ం} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ం} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{◌ం} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{నమస్కారం}  ·  \te{రేపు} \te{కలుద్దాం}  ·  \te{ధన్యవాదములు}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌ం} three times, humming the nasal at the end of the syllable as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{◌ం} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌ం}? What does it add to the syllable before it? (\textbf{A nasal.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ca]{\te{చ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S112-letter-ca}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{స} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{చ}}
\textbf{\te{చ}} — \emph{ca}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{c}, it is \textbf{ca}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{చ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{పని} \te{చేయు}} \emph{pani cēyu} — to work (lit. \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{తెలుగు} \te{వచ్చు}} \emph{nāku telugu vaccu} — 'I know Telugu'
  \item \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} \emph{dayacēsi} — please (dayacēsi
  \item \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} — please forgive / sorry
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{చ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{చ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{చ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{చ} three times, saying \emph{ca} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{చ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{చ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ca}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
